extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, employers, and workplace safety/compliance professionals (OSHA HCS stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and final-rule guidance on Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) labeling, pictogram, transportation, bulk-shipment, SDS, and label-update requirements for shipped and workplace chemical containers. Covers what must appear on labels, permissible exemptions, electronic transmission of labels, and procedures for updating labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written hazard communication program as employee exposure record (1910.1020 reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: A written hazard communication program that contains a list of the hazardous chemicals known to be present using a product identifier referenced on the appropriate safety data sheet is classified as an employee exposure record within the meaning of §1910.1020.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such a program is an exposure record under §1910.1020, OSHA's access requirements apply (assure that employees are provided records in a reasonable time, location, and manner; employers assume costs of records provision to employees and their representatives). §1910.120(l)(1) (HAZWOPER emergency-response plan) is less relevant because it lacks exposure-access procedures and is intended for emergency response only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labels on shipped containers — required information and exemptions (paragraph (f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (f)(1) specifies what information is required on shipped containers of hazardous chemicals and provides that hazards not otherwise classified (HNOCs) do not have to be addressed on these containers. OSHA proposed and finalizes that hazards resulting from a reaction with other chemicals that are not required on the label per the clarified classification language in paragraph (d)(1)(ii) are exempt from shipped-container labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information about downstream hazards must still appear on Section 2 (Hazard(s) Identification) of the SDS and be incorporated in worker training where applicable. Omitting downstream-reaction hazards from the shipping label focuses the label on immediate hazards associated with the chemical in the container and minimizes over-warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include 'distributor' in (f)(1) label text
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition of the word 'distributor' to the third sentence of paragraph (f)(1) to make the paragraph consistent with the first sentence and reflect distributors' roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No adverse comments were received on this inclusion; OSHA is finalizing that textual addition as proposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible party U.S. address and telephone number (f)(1)(vi) / Appendix D clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The address and telephone number of the chemical manufacturer, importer, or other responsible party required in Section 1 of the SDS (Identification) must be United States domestic (U.S. address and U.S. telephone number).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies the pre-existing Appendix D requirement and the 2016 LOI that the importer (first business with employees in the U.S. to receive foreign-produced hazardous chemicals for U.S. distribution) is the responsible party for HCS compliance and must use a U.S. address/phone. It is not a new substantive requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release-for-shipment date on label — not required in final rule
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA proposed requiring the label include the date a chemical is released for shipment, but after stakeholder comment OSHA concluded this is unnecessary and is not adopting that requirement in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include: date information already available via other means (lot/manufacturing dates), limited label space, potential confusion with other regulatory dates (DOT, FDA, expiration/requalification), burdens of changing processes or preprinted labels, and lack of GHS/international requirement. Stakeholders may track inventory by other methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation labeling heading and statutory citation update (f)(5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (f)(5) specifies label requirements that apply to the transport of hazardous chemicals from workplace to workplace; OSHA added the heading 'Transportation' and updated the Hazardous Materials Transportation Act citation from 49 U.S.C. 1801 et seq. to 49 U.S.C. 5101 et seq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical correction only; the transportation labeling requirements remain aligned with DOT/transportation law where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bulk shipments labeling options and requirement to choose option (f)(5)(ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: For bulk shipments (tanker trucks, rail cars, intermodal containers), labels may either be on the immediate container or transmitted with shipping papers, bills of lading, or by other technological or electronic means so that the information is immediately available in printed form to workers on the receiving end of the shipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA revised the text to require (must) that the label preparer choose one of the provided options and to require agreement from the recipient if labels are transmitted by means other than a physical label on the bulk container or printed form. The intent is to ensure the label is immediately available to the receiver while allowing electronic options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic transmission of labels for bulk shipments — recipient opt-in and opt-out rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If electronic transmission is used for bulk shipment product labels, the recipient of the shipment must agree (opt-in) to receive labels by an alternate (electronic) method. A downstream user/recipient may opt-out at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the recipient opts out, the shipper must ensure a product label is on each bulk shipment or provide a hard copy of the product label with shipping papers/bills of lading. Electronic transmission may be accomplished via computer systems, facsimile, or bar/QR code so long as the product label is immediately available in printed form at the receiving end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure electronic labels are immediately available in printed form
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic or technological transmission of bulk-shipment labels is permissible only if the information is immediately available in printed form to workers on the receiving end of the shipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA added recipient consent and clarified that a single electronic transmission for multiple shipments is not acceptable if it would not provide the label to the receiver at time of delivery. The recipient must explicitly accept the electronic method to ensure printed availability at delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance of DOT pictogram together with HCS pictogram (Appendix C / (f)(5)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a DOT pictogram appears on a shipped container, the pictogram specified in Appendix C.4 of the HCS for the same hazard is allowed but is not required on the HCS label; OSHA deleted the prior provision that prohibited the HCS pictogram where DOT pictograms appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This harmonizes with DOT's updated view that HCS pictograms do not conflict with DOT pictograms. OSHA's text clarifies that inclusion of the HCS pictogram is optional and that the end user need not add the HCS pictogram upon receipt, provided the DOT pictogram is present and not defaced. OSHA rejected suggestions to require HCS pictograms be in the same field of view as DOT markings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label Updates / Relabeling optional accommodation for products released for shipment (f)(11))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under paragraph (f)(11) manufacturers, importers, distributors, or employers who become newly aware of significant information regarding hazards must revise labels within six months and ensure labels on containers shipped after that time contain the new information. OSHA proposed and finalizes an optional accommodation: chemicals 'released for shipment' and awaiting future distribution need not be relabeled provided the chemical manufacturer or importer provides an updated label for each individual container with each shipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA clarifies this accommodation is optional (manufacturers/distributors may choose to relabel instead). OSHA revised paragraph title from 'Release for Shipment' to 'Label Updates' to reflect purpose. The originator is responsible to ensure updated labels accompany shipments. The accommodation addresses long distribution cycles and safety concerns associated with relabeling existing packaged stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and practical considerations regarding relabeling existing stock
rubrics_metrics.description: Relabeling or repackaging existing stock at warehouses or distribution facilities can pose occupational safety and health risks (e.g., opening secure packaging may result in chemical exposures) and may be impractical for long-distribution-cycle products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The optional labeling accommodation is intended to avoid these risks while still providing up-to-date information to downstream users; manufacturers may opt out of the accommodation if they prefer to relabel prior to shipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden, liability, and process-flexibility concerns about shipping updated labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters expressed concerns that shipping unaffixed labels places the burden on downstream users to apply updated labels, raises liability issues, and may not ensure relabeling actually occurs; commenters also asked for flexibility in how/when to send updated labels (electronically or in advance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA responds that the accommodation is optional, originators are responsible to ensure labels accompany shipments, and relying solely on SDS or sending labels separately would fail to ensure downstream users have updated labels at time of receipt. If originators are concerned about liability or process burdens, they may relabel at shipment instead of using the accommodation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and flexibility of label placement (paragraph (c) definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's definition of 'label' in paragraph (c) allows that labels may be affixed to, printed on, or attached to the immediate container (or outside packaging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests to alter wording to explicitly allow 'attach or affix' were denied as unnecessary because the definition already allows various placement methods; OSHA maintains the current flexible definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDS availability versus provision of copies — access rules under HCS and 1910.1020
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCS does not require employers to provide copies of SDSs to employees, only immediate access. However, where an SDS constitutes an exposure record under 29 CFR 1910.1020(c)(5), then 1910.1020's access provisions (including opportunity to examine and copy and employer assumption of copying costs) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction informs whether employers must allow copying/provide copies versus only ensuring immediate availability.
